title: During World War II, the psychologist B. F. Skinner trained pigeons to steer bombs

cover.alt: A grey feral rock dove, the common city pigeon, with an iridescent green and purple neck, standing on the ground.

body: Skinner studied operant conditioning: behaviour that is rewarded gets repeated. In Project Pigeon he used food rewards to train pigeons to recognise a target and peck at its image. Three lenses in the nose of a glider bomb projected the view ahead onto a pivoting screen, with one to three birds in front of it. If the bomb drifted off course, the target’s image slid towards the edge, the pecks pushed the screen, and sensors turned that movement into steering. A wartime research committee put $25,000 into it, yet, as Skinner put it, no one would take the team seriously, and electronics eventually took over the job.

slides.text: Training rewarded faster and faster pecking with food, until the birds kept up a furious rate.

slides.heading: Put the pigeon programme in order
items: Navy revives it as Project Orcon
Skinner wins an Ig Nobel Prize
slides.explanation: Orcon ran from 1948 until 1953, when electronic guidance proved reliable. The Ig Nobel Peace Prize followed in 2024, awarded to Skinner posthumously.

slides.question: When the Navy revived the idea in 1948, it called it Project Orcon. What did Orcon stand for?
slides.explanation: Organic control: a living guidance system. Early electronic guidance worked in a similar way, with signals and processors in place of the birds.

slides.heading: A prize, eight decades late
slides.text: In 2024 Skinner was awarded the Ig Nobel Peace Prize for the project. His daughter Julie Vargas accepted it on his behalf, thanking the organisers ‘for finally acknowledging his most important contribution’.
